query: For HfNbTaTiZr refractory high-entropy alloy, earlier studies separately examined tensile creep at 1250 °C, microhardness changes during cold rolling, elastic moduli from 293 to 1100 K, and hardening after aging at 600–800 °C. However, these findings do not provide a unified explanation of the alloy’s stress–strain and thermoelastic behavior. Thermal expansion is also relevant because mismatch can produce thermal stresses during composite solidification and potentially affect strength. What single testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain the unresolved behavior? Specify a controlled comparison that would isolate the governing cause, observations predicted relative to a baseline, the relevant temperature and response boundaries, how the earlier findings support the hypothesis, and an observation that would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: In HfNbTaTiZr, controlled aging at different temperatures induces varying degrees of thermal expansion mismatch among the constituent elements. This mismatch creates residual lattice stresses that alter dislocation core structures, thereby unifying the alloy’s anomalous stress–strain and thermoelastic responses observed across diverse tests.
generation.material_initial_state: A homogenized single‐phase refractory high-entropy alloy (BCC structured HfNbTaTiZr) that has undergone a uniform deformation history (e.g., cold rolling) and solution annealing.
generation.intervention: Apply a series of controlled aging treatments at selected temperatures (e.g., 600°C, 700°C, 800°C, and a higher temperature such as 900°C for comparison) while keeping the pre-aging deformation history constant.
generation.conditions: Temperature treatments in the aging range of 600–800°C (with an additional control at 900°C) under identical atmospheric and processing conditions; subsequent mechanical testing (tensile and creep) performed at temperatures spanning from room temperature to 1250°C to capture stress–strain and thermoelastic behavior.
generation.structural_mediator: Residual lattice stresses induced by thermal expansion mismatch between the constituent elements, which modify the local dislocation core structure and effective Peierls barrier.
generation.mechanism: Varying aging temperatures change the degree of thermal expansion mismatch, thereby generating distinct residual internal stresses. These stresses alter dislocation core widths and pinning characteristics, unifying observations of unusual creep, microhardness, and elastic modulus variations. In essence, the lattice-level stress field arising from differential thermal expansion modifies dislocation mobility and accounts for both the mechanical strengthening (or softening) and the thermoelastic response.
generation.predicted_outcome: Aging treatments that enhance the thermal expansion mismatch (within the 600–800°C range) will lead to increased yield strength and elastic modulus relative to a baseline (unaged or low-temperature aged) state, as well as altered strain hardening behavior. Deviations from baseline mechanical properties should correlate with measurable changes in lattice parameters (indicative of internal stresses) from XRD or similar techniques.
generation.baseline: The alloy processed with an identical cold rolling history but solution annealed with minimal subsequent aging, thereby exhibiting lower or nominal levels of residual lattice stress from thermal expansion mismatch.
generation.boundary: The hypothesis is expected to hold in the aging temperature regime where thermal expansion mismatch can be tuned (approximately 600°C to 800°C). Outside this window (e.g., at very high temperatures like 900°C or below aging conditions), competing phenomena such as precipitation or insufficient lattice stress may override the mechanism.
generation.uncertainty: The precise quantitative relationship between aging temperature–induced thermal expansion mismatch and the resulting changes in dislocation core structure (and thus mechanical properties) is uncertain. It may also be challenging to completely decouple the effects of precipitation or segregation from those of pure thermal mismatch without detailed microstructural characterization.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare multiple batches of HfNbTaTiZr alloy with an identical prior deformation history. Subject each batch to aging treatments at 600°C, 700°C, 800°C, and 900°C, ensuring all other processing variables (atmosphere, time, cooling rate) are controlled. After aging, perform mechanical tests (tensile and creep) at a range of temperatures (including room temperature, intermediate, and near 1250°C) and characterize the lattice parameters using X-ray diffraction and transmission electron microscopy to assess residual lattice stresses and dislocation core structures.
measurements: Yield strength and elastic modulus from tensile tests
Lattice parameter shifts and internal stress estimations via XRD
Dislocation structure and density via TEM
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If systematic variations in mechanical properties (yield strength, elastic modulus, strain hardening) and lattice parameters do not correlate with the aging temperature (i.e., if aging at 600–800°C yields no significant differences from the baseline or if any observed changes can be solely attributed to precipitation or segregation effects), then the hypothesis that thermal expansion mismatch is the governing cause is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: There have been extensive efforts to investigate the strengthening mechanisms in RHEAs (, , ), and the dominant strengthening mechanism in single-phase RHEAs was mostly reported to be the solid solution hardening (). However, unlike conventional alloys, quantifying the effect of solid solution strengthening on HEAs is challenging because of the inability to distinguish between solvent and solute atoms. There are two sources of solid solution hardening in single-phase RHEAs: (i) The random mixing of major alloying elements in the crystal lattice gives rise to local fluctuations and lattice distortions, which introduce energy barriers against dislocation motions and serve as a substitutional solid solution–like strengthening mechanism (); and (ii) Interstitial impurities, such as oxygen and nitrogen, also create high degrees of lattice distortions () and chemical fluctuations, thereby serving as an interstitial solid solution-like strengthening mechanism. reading.lever: Control aging temperatures to induce varying thermal expansion mismatch while maintaining identical prior deformation history.
reading.why: This approach isolates thermal expansion-induced lattice stress effects on dislocation core structures to unify stress–strain and thermoelastic behavior.
